summary:
Earth Observation satellites have tracked active fires for over two decades. However, the operational retirement of MODIS (1 km resolution) and its replacement by VIIRS (375 m resolution) creates a critical discontinuity: VIIRS detects substantially more smaller, cooler fires than MODIS, making raw historical comparisons invalid.

To solve this, we developed PyroLens—a web application that bridges MODIS and VIIRS satellite records into a unified, cross-sensor Harmonized Burning Activity Calendar. Rather than displaying fragmented points, PyroLens aggregates thermal anomalies into a 0.25° spatiotemporal grid, applies climatological normalization across satellite orbits, and computes a standardized Burning Activity Index (BAI).

PyroLens features an interactive MapLibre + deck.gl map with NASA GIBS true-color overlays, anomaly detection against historical baselines, automated daily FIRMS sync, and an explainable seasonal Fire Likelihood Prediction & Verification Engine. By locking predictions before observation windows close and evaluating live accuracy via confusion matrices, PyroLens empowers fire managers, researchers, and communities with trustworthy, science-grade fire intelligence.
details:
1. What does it do or how does it work?

PyroLens harmonizes NASA active-fire observations across two sensor generations into a single comparable dataset:

  1. Quality Control & Ingestion: Accepts historical NASA FIRMS CSV archives and live Near-Real-Time (NRT) API feeds, eliminating duplicate overlapping detections and rejecting invalid geometries.
  2. Constellation Normalization: Normalizes raw detections by operational satellite counts (Terra + Aqua for MODIS; Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21 for VIIRS) to prevent new satellite launches from falsely resembling increased fire activity.
  3. Monthly Harmonization Scaling: Calculates monthly VIIRS-to-MODIS scaling ratios r(m) during overlapping operational years (2012–present) across active cell counts, Fire Radiative Power (FRP), and spatial cluster counts.
  4. Burning Activity Index (BAI): Translates multi-sensor observations into a robust, scale-invariant index (0–100) combining fire counts, radiative energy, and spatial clustering.
    BAI = 100 × (w1 × Ĥ + w2 × F̂ + w3 × Ĉ)
  5. Calendar Engine & Anomaly Detection: Computes a day-of-year climatology (±7-day window) across all historical years, classifying daily activity into percentiles (Low, Moderate, High, Extreme) and flagging anomalous spikes (>90th percentile) and critical consecutive-day periods.
  6. Fire Likelihood Prediction & Verification: Generates seasonal baseline likelihood predictions for future dates over spatial grids (0.10°, 0.25°, 0.50°) using day-of-year circular wrap-around windows. Predictions are immutable: once created, they cannot be modified. After the target date's satellite observations become available, PyroLens measures prediction accuracy against live FIRMS observations, outputting True Positives (TP), False Positives (FP), False Negatives (FN), True Negatives (TN), Precision, Recall, and F1 scores.

2. What benefits does it have & what is the intended impact?

  • Solves the Sensor Transition Problem: Eliminates the misleading jump in apparent fire activity caused by VIIRS's higher spatial resolution (375 m vs 1 km).
  • True Zero vs Missing Data Distinction: Differentiates days with true zero fire from days with missing satellite overpasses or cloud/smoke obstruction, preventing false reassurance.
  • Explainable Forecasting: Unlike black-box machine learning models, PyroLens uses an explainable, climatologically grounded recurrence model verified against live satellite telemetry.
  • Actionable for Resource Managers: Enables park rangers, regional fire authorities, and climate scientists to detect early/late burning seasons, export GeoJSON boundaries, and prepare before peak fire weeks.

3. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS 4 (light/dark theme tokens).
  • Mapping & Spatial Visualization: MapLibre GL, @deck.gl/core, @deck.gl/layers (Polygon, Scatterplot, Heatmap), Canvas API.
  • Backend & Automation: Vercel Serverless Functions (api/firms/live.ts), Python 3.10, GitHub Actions CI/CD (automated daily sync).
  • Data Processing & Testing: Vitest (113 automated unit tests), Pandas, GeoJSON, HTML5 LocalStorage persistence.

4. How is your project creative?

  • Harmonized Burning Activity Calendar: Reimagines satellite tables as an intuitive GitHub-style multi-year heatmap, allowing users to spot two decades of seasonal shifts in seconds.
  • Sensor-Harmonized Deck.gl Rendering: Hotspots adaptively render by detection age (freshly detected fires pulse brightly) or FRP intensity, with confidence encoded into stroke styling rather than conflicting hues.
  • Closed-Window Verification Framework: Pioneers strict immutability in public fire forecasting: predictions must be created before the target date and remain locked, ensuring objective, tamper-proof precision/recall measurement against live satellite data.

5. What factors did your team consider?

  • Physical Satellite Characteristics: Spatial footprint differences, varying overpass times (Terra morning/night vs Aqua/VIIRS afternoon/night), scan angles, and saturation brightness temperatures.
  • Client Browser Performance: Large raw archives (up to 1.4 GB) are processed in chunks or through automated cloud summaries, keeping client browser memory lightweight while supporting full local CSV imports.
  • Public Safety & Ethics: Implemented explicit scientific disclaimers confirming that satellite thermal anomalies are not ground-confirmed wildfire perimeters and must never supersede official emergency evacuation warnings.
